vocabulary.cultural_note: A vessel for burning incense, from a plain clay pot in a house to worked metal in a temple. Incense is offered daily, and it is also used to clear and settle a room before anything else happens in it. In many homes the first act of the morning is lighting it. Outdoors the same thing is done at a much larger scale, burning juniper in a kiln-shaped hearth at a monastery gate or on a pass.

vocabulary.en_definition: India — the country immediately south, over the Himalaya. A great many of the Tibetans a learner meets outside Tibet live there, so it comes up constantly.
Inside. Useful once you have found the building and still cannot find the thing.
The specific metal rather than metal in general: what a blade, a hinge, a nail or a stove door is made of. This is the blacksmith's material, not the silversmith's.
The particular position someone holds: this trade, at this place, for this employer. Narrower than work in general.
The temple at the center of the old town, and the point everything else in Lhasa is described in relation to. Ask the way to it from anywhere in the old streets and somebody can point.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The Jokhang is the temple at the center of the old town and the point everything else in Lhasa is described in relation to. It holds the statue pilgrims cross the plateau to stand in front of, and its courtyard flagstones are worn into hollows by people prostrating in the same spots for centuries. Founded in the seventh century, it is far older than anything else standing in the city, and it faces west rather than towards the mountains behind it. The smoke on the approach is juniper burning in the two kilns outside the doors, and the street running clockwise around it is the Barkhor, so temple, market and pilgrim circuit are the same few hundred metres of ground.

vocabulary.en_definition: The thick white smoke of juniper branches burnt in the morning — at a monastery gate, on a hilltop, at the top of a pass. The smell of it reaches you well before you can see where it is coming from, and it is one of the things people remember longest about being here.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sang*. The བ is a silent prefix — *sang*, not "b-sang".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Juniper smoke is the offering, not the fire: the point is that it rises and spreads. It is burnt at first light at monasteries and by households on their own roofs, so a Tibetan town at dawn has smoke going up from a dozen places at once. Fresh branches are burnt in a low masonry hearth, often with tsampa, butter or barley thrown on top, and travelers burn it again on reaching the top of a pass. Juniper grows slowly at these altitudes and good branches are carried a long way to reach the place they are burnt.

vocabulary.en_definition: The key to your room. It is often kept at the desk rather than carried, and handed over each time you come back in.
vocabulary.thl_note: *demik*. The ལ is a silent prefix — not "l-de".

vocabulary.en_definition: A long scarf of thin white silk or cotton, offered with both hands. It is given on arrival, on departure, at weddings, at the start of a journey, and at almost every occasion in between.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khatak*. The བ prefix and the final ས are silent. This is one of section 8.4's anchored forms — if the generated THL disagrees with known-forms.json, the table wins.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A khata is a ceremonial scarf offered to show respect, welcome, gratitude or good wishes, and it marks almost any occasion that matters. It is given to teachers and elders, to a couple marrying, to a guest arriving and to someone leaving, and draped over statues and photographs. It is offered with both hands and a slight bow, and the person receiving it very often puts it straight back around the giver's neck, so it travels in both directions. White is the standard color, associated with sincerity and good intention; a finer one in five colors is the more formal offering.

vocabulary.en_definition: Kindness in the specific sense of goodness done to you by somebody else: a debt of care rather than a personality trait.
vocabulary.thl_note: *katin*. དྲ is a single voiced sound *dr*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: This word sits underneath the everyday Tibetan 'thank you' that District 1 taught — the thanks is built on it. What it names is not the favor somebody did but the kindness they showed in doing it, and the same word covers what parents give a child. With it comes the idea that such kindness is owed back: repaying kindness is a standing obligation rather than an optional generosity. That is part of why thanks in Tibetan can carry more weight than the English word does, and why between people who are close it is often left unsaid, because it is assumed.

vocabulary.en_definition: A walk clockwise around something held sacred — a temple, a monastery, a mountain, a whole city. The word covers both the walk and the path it follows.
vocabulary.thl_note: *korra*. The ས is a silent prefix. This is a section 8.4 anchor — known-forms.json wins over anything generated.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A kora is a walk made clockwise around something held sacred — a temple, a monastery, a mountain, a whole city — done as an act of devotion. That does not stop it also being the daily exercise and the place where people meet and talk; the devotional and the social are not separate here. Some koras take twenty minutes; the circuit of Mount Kailash takes several days, and pilgrims who measure their length along the ground rather than walking take weeks. The Bön tradition, which runs alongside Buddhism in Tibet and is older, goes the other way round, anticlockwise, and going the wrong way at a Buddhist site is the most visible mistake a visitor makes and the easiest to put right.

vocabulary.en_definition: A lake. Most of the big plateau lakes are salt, and the largest of them sit above 4,500 metres.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tsho*. The མ is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Several of the great lakes are held sacred and are walked around rather than swum in or fished, a walk round the shore that takes days on foot. They are also extraordinarily blue, being high, cold and clear, which is why photographs of them look adjusted when they are not. Some freeze hard enough in winter to be crossed on the ice.

vocabulary.en_definition: A teacher — someone trained and recognised by their own teachers as qualified to instruct others. It is a title for standing and training, not another word for 'monk'.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Visitors routinely use this word for any monk they meet, which is roughly like calling everyone in a hospital 'doctor'. Most monks are not lamas, and a lama need not be a monk: some are monastics, some are married householders, and some are recognised as the rebirth of a previous teacher — that last group are properly called tulkus, and English writing about Tibet conflates the two words more often than not. The title carries real authority within a community, so it is not applied loosely by Tibetans. If you are unsure what to call a monk you have just met, the ordinary word for monk is the safe one.

vocabulary.en_definition: A language — the general word, used for Tibetan, English, Chinese or any other. It is the noun that the courtyard conversation runs on.
Cold mung-bean noodle, cut into slippery strips and dressed with chilli, vinegar and garlic. It is eaten standing at a stall rather than sitting in a restaurant.
vocabulary.thl_note: *laphing*. A Chinese loan (涼粉 liángfěn), so the syllables carry no Tibetan meaning.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Laping is the thing eaten between things — a cold mung-bean noodle under chilli oil, bought standing at a stall in the middle of the afternoon. The stalls cluster around the Barkhor and are run overwhelmingly by women, and the chilli on it is far hotter than anything else in this kitchen. The noodle is a set jelly rather than a dried strand: mung-bean starch cooked to a paste, left overnight to firm up in a tray, then cut into ribbons or shaved into curls. It came in from Chinese cooking and has been absorbed so thoroughly that Lhasa now argues about whose version is correct.

vocabulary.en_definition: Last night, yesterday evening. The one arrangement here that is not simply the two obvious words joined, so it is worth hearing on its own.
Later, at some point after this. It is deliberately vague, which is exactly what makes it useful: it lets you leave a conversation without fixing a time to anything.
vocabulary.thl_note: *djela*. རྗ is a single *j*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Leather or hide: the material rather than the animal. Boots, bags, ropes and saddle gear are made of it, and the word comes back in the workshop district where it is worked.
Left. Half of the pair that carries almost every direction you will be given.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yönchhok*. The ག of གཡོན is silent — གཡ is a single y sound, not "g-yon".

vocabulary.en_definition: Less: a smaller quantity than the one offered.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nyungtsam*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Tibetan opera: a sung and danced drama performed outdoors, with masks, a narrator and a chorus. A performance runs for hours and sometimes across days.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lhamo*. ལྷ is a single voiceless *lh*, one sound, not "l" plus "h".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tibetan opera is played in the round on flat ground, with the audience sitting on all sides and coming and going as they please. The stories come from history and from well-known tales and everyone already knows how they end, so the audience eats, talks and plays cards throughout. A narrator sets each scene in verse and a chorus answers the singers, and masks and color do the work a costume would do elsewhere, telling you who a character is before a word is sung. Troupes travel to summer festivals, and a performance runs for hours and sometimes across days.

vocabulary.en_definition: Lhasa: the city this walk moves through, and the source of the variety of Tibetan taught here.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Lhasa is the city Tibetans mean when they say the city — the seat of the Jokhang temple and the destination of pilgrims from every part of the plateau. Its old town is arranged in rings around that temple, and the street circling it is pilgrim route and main market at once. It sits at about three and a half thousand metres on the Kyichu river, high enough that most arrivals spend their first day short of breath, and its speech is what standard spoken Tibetan means.

vocabulary.en_definition: The lock on a door — the object, not the act of using it. Take it together with the key from earlier in the district: one is the thing you are handed at the desk, the other is the thing it fits.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gochak*. Literally "door-iron".

vocabulary.en_definition: Losar, the Tibetan New Year: the largest festival of the year, on the first day of the first Tibetan month, which puts it in February or March.
vocabulary.thl_note: *losar*. The ག of གསར is a silent prefix.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Losar is the largest festival of the year, and its shape is fixed: the first day at home, the second visiting, the third going out. The days before are for cleaning the house out completely and for a noodle soup on the eve, with small objects hidden in the dumplings for everyone's amusement but the finder's. New prayer flags go up over the roofs and the greeting is exchanged with everybody. Because the date comes out of the lunisolar calendar it moves in the Western year, and it does not always fall with the Chinese New Year.

vocabulary.en_definition: The lotus flower, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The lotus stands for purity that comes through the mud rather than by avoiding it — a flower that grows up out of mud and opens clean, without a mark on it. Almost every buddha and bodhisattva in Tibetan painting is seated or standing on one. When you next look at a thangka, look at what the figure is standing on: it is nearly always this.

vocabulary.en_definition: Said of a sound that carries: a drum, a crowd, a voice across a field. Not a complaint in this district.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ke chhenpo*. སྐ is a single unaspirated *k*; the ས is a silent prefix and the final ད of སྐད is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: The knee-high carved table that stands in front of the wall cushions. It is the surface everything happens on — tea, food, work — and it is carried to wherever the people are rather than staying put.
vocabulary.thl_note: *choktse*. This is the *chogtse* the spec names.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The chogtse is built to be used by people sitting on cushions rather than on chairs, which sets its height, and it is made light enough for one person to pick up and move. The good ones are wooden, jointed without nails, and painted on the front and sides in strong mineral colors with lotus, dragon and cloud designs; a household will often have a plain one for every day and a painted one that comes out for guests. Because the table travels round the room, a Tibetan room has no fixed place where meals happen. Those painted panels are one of the last everyday settings in which Tibetan decorative painting is still done by hand rather than printed. District 3 taught the ordinary word for a table, and this is deliberately not that word.

vocabulary.en_definition: Whether things are falling your way — in the dice, in the races, in the day. Spoken of as something that comes and goes rather than something a person owns.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sö de*. Both prefixes (བ, བ) are silent; the ད of བསོད is silent and colours the vowel to ö.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Festival grounds and teahouses both run on a dice game played over a pad of yak leather stuffed with wool: a wooden cup is shaken, slammed down hard and lifted, and counters made from old coins move around a ring of cowrie shells. It is played for money, mostly by men, and the noise is the point — players shout a set chant as the cup comes down, and slamming, shouting and sweeping an opponent's counters aside are all good form rather than bad manners. The vocabulary that grows around it is ordinary and unmysterious: a good day, a bad one, a run that turns, a game that comes right at the end. The word belongs to that world and to the weather, not to anything a specialist would be consulted about.

vocabulary.en_definition: Lung, 'wind': the first of the three factors Tibetan medicine uses to describe a working body. It names a concept in that system, not a body part.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Lung, wind, is the first of the three factors Sowa Rigpa uses to describe a working body — the one covering movement: breath, circulation, quickness of mind. It is also the word people reach for in ordinary speech for restlessness, anxiety or sleeplessness, so you will hear it well outside a clinic. The tradition states health as the balance of lung with tripa and beken, and illness as their disturbance, with diet and season discussed as causes within that account. This describes how the tradition explains a body; it says nothing about yours.

vocabulary.en_definition: A string of beads used to keep count of recitations, worn on the wrist or held in the hand. You will see them everywhere, often moving while their owner is doing something else entirely.
vocabulary.thl_note: *threngwa*. ཕྲ is a single aspirated *thr* — not "ph" then "r".
vocabulary.cultural_note: A mala is what a recitation is counted on, and you will see them everywhere, often moving while their owner is doing something else entirely. One bead is passed for each repetition, worked through with the thumb, and at the head the string is turned back rather than crossed. The standard string has 108 beads and a larger head bead, with small counter strings hanging off some malas for keeping track of completed rounds. Bone, wood, seed and stone are all ordinary materials, and a mala moving in somebody's hand during a conversation is not inattention.

vocabulary.en_definition: A man. One of the first words you need to describe someone you have just met to somebody else.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kyepa*. The ས prefix and the final ས are both silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: A flat stone carved with a written mantra and left beside a path. They gather into long walls and heaps at passes, river crossings and the edges of villages.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mani do*. ཎ is the retroflex n of the Sanskrit mantra, pronounced as an ordinary *n*.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A mani stone is a flat stone carved with a mantra and left beside a path, added and never taken away. They gather into walls that grow at the rate of the traffic past them, so some are hundreds of metres long and centuries deep, with the oldest stones buried inside. Carving them is a trade as well as an act of devotion: carvers work at the roadside and are paid to add a stone on someone else's behalf. Walkers pass with the wall on their right, which is why a mani wall down the middle of a path has a lane on either side of it.

vocabulary.en_definition: A short fixed formula, said over and over, usually under the breath and counted on a mala. On the kora it is the sound underneath everything else: hundreds of people murmuring, none of them loudly.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nghak*. སྔ is a single sound *ng*; there is no "s" before it.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A mantra is a short fixed formula said over and over, and on the kora it is the sound underneath everything else. It is done while doing other things — walking, waiting, sitting on a bus — which is why it can take a visitor several days to notice how much of it is going on. The one heard most is the six-syllable mantra associated with Avalokiteshvara, the figure of compassion, and it is the same text carved into mani stones and rolled up inside prayer wheels. It is counted rather than simply repeated: a mala of a hundred and eight beads is worked round, and people keep running totals over years. The syllables are Sanskrit rather than Tibetan and are kept in an approximated pronunciation rather than translated, because the sound itself is held to be the working part.

vocabulary.en_definition: A map. Worth carrying and worth producing: somebody who cannot explain the way in words will very often take the map out of your hands and put a finger on it.
The market. You spent the whole of District 5 in one; this is the word for asking your way back to it.
A heavy burrowing rodent of the grassland. It stands upright at the mouth of its hole and whistles when something comes near.

Marriage, as a thing rather than as something you do. It is here mainly because whether you are married is one of the first questions a stranger will ask you, put without any of the awkwardness an English speaker expects.
A face worn by a performer, made of painted cloth, papier-mâché or carved wood. It announces which character you are looking at from the far side of a field.
vocabulary.thl_note: *bak*. འ is a silent prefix. One syllable.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A mask announces which character you are looking at from the far side of a field, and color is the main code. A blue mask, a white mask and a half-red mask each signal a particular kind of character to an audience that grew up watching. They fall into two families: the flat cloth ones of opera, and the heavy carved and painted ones worn in monastic masked dance. The dance masks belong to the monastery that holds them and are stored rather than displayed, brought out for dances that fall on set days in the calendar — town events, watched by everyone.

vocabulary.en_definition: Maybe, perhaps. The softener for when yes and no are both too strong — an invitation you have not decided about, a plan that may not happen. It leaves the question open without committing you to anything.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chik chheena* — གཅིག is *chik*, not "g-chig".

vocabulary.en_definition: Meat in general. It matters more here than in most cuisines, because very little else grows at this height.

Sangye Menla, the Medicine Buddha: the blue figure at the center of a Tibetan medical room, a sprig of myrobalan in one hand and a bowl in the other. Where a clinic elsewhere might hang a diagram, this is what is on the wall.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Sangye Menla, the Medicine Buddha, is the blue figure at the center of a Tibetan medical room, where a clinic elsewhere might hang a diagram. He holds a sprig of myrobalan in one hand and a bowl in the other, and the lapis blue is the same in every painting, which makes him easy to identify. The tradition holds that the Four Tantras were taught by him in a city of medicine surrounded by the plants they describe, so the textbook and the image on the wall are one story told twice. Students of Tibetan medicine have traditionally begun their training with him rather than with anatomy, and paintings often show eight such figures together rather than a single one. Describing that is as far as this card goes; the practice belongs to the people who keep it.

vocabulary.en_definition: A menu. Not every small restaurant has one, and where it exists it may be painted on the wall rather than handed to you, so asking for it is a reasonable opening move either way.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshetho*, "vegetable list" — the same ཐོ as ལོ་ཐོ, a calendar.

vocabulary.en_definition: Midday, noon. It is a stretch of the day rather than a point on a clock, and it fills the gap between morning and afternoon in the sequence you are learning here.
Middle, center. The middle of a square, the middle of the road, or the center of a town as against its edges — all three take this word.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kyi* — the ད is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: Midnight. Less immediately useful than the other time words and here to complete them, though it earns its place in District 13, where long-distance buses leave at hours like this one.
Milk. It goes into sweet tea, and comes from the same animals as the butter.
A mirror. In a plain guesthouse it hangs by the courtyard tap rather than in your room, because that is where people wash and comb their hair, so it is a thing you go to rather than a thing you have.
vocabulary.thl_note: *shego*. Literally a "glass door".

vocabulary.en_definition: A dumpling, steamed or fried, filled with meat or vegetables. If one dish stands in for the whole cuisine, it is this one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mokmok*, two identical syllables. The ག of the first syllable is not heard as a separate consonant.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The momo is the dish that stands in for the whole cuisine: a dumpling, steamed or fried, filled with minced meat and onion or with greens and cheese. They belong to New Year, holidays and visitors rather than to a quiet Tuesday, because they are made in batches by several people at a table talking. The dough is rolled and pleated by hand and how neat the pleats are is noticed, and the same dumpling under a similar name turns up all across the Himalaya and well beyond it.

vocabulary.en_definition: A monastery. It appears here only as a landmark to steer by; the vocabulary for what is inside one arrives in District 8.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gönpa* — the ད is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: Monday, the Moon's day, as in English and as in the French lundi.
Money. The general word, for what changes hands rather than for any particular note or coin.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nghü*. The ད is silent. It is also the word for the metal silver — see `silver`.

vocabulary.en_definition: A man who has taken monastic vows and lives in a monastery community, in maroon robes. Monks staff the buildings a visitor walks through, and it is normal to speak to them.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thraapa*. གྲ is a single voiced *dr*, and the ྭ under it is silent — not "g-r-wa".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Men enter a monastery at any age, sometimes as children, and the community is a working institution as much as a place of retreat: monks run the buildings, keep the accounts, teach, cook, and look after visitors. Training is built on memorisation and on formal debate — the shouting and hand-clapping in a monastery courtyard is a debate in progress, not an argument. The robes are maroon with yellow, rather than the saffron worn further south. Monastic populations today are far smaller than the buildings were designed to hold, which is why some great monasteries feel empty.

vocabulary.en_definition: Morning. It is a piece of time you can talk about, not a greeting: there is no separate good morning to learn.
vocabulary.thl_note: *shookpa*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Your mother, and the word you use to introduce her. Note that speaking about somebody else's mother is more formal in Tibetan than speaking about your own; the register is not optional politeness here.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ama lak*. ལགས is not a suffix the learner adds or drops at will — it is part of the word.

vocabulary.en_definition: A painting made directly on the wall, as against a thangka, which is painted on cloth and rolls up. Old halls are covered in them floor to ceiling, and centuries of butter lamps have made them far darker than they were painted.
vocabulary.thl_note: *depri*. ལྡ is a single *d* — the ལ is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: Mutton. Sheep are kept high and wide across the plateau, so this is the other everyday meat.
A person's name. Asking for someone else's name and offering your own are handled by separate fixed phrases in this district, so you are never asked to pick between them yourself.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ming*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Near, close by. It is the answer you are hoping for, though it stretches further on foot than you might like.
A necklace. At a market stall this almost always means a strung line of stones — coral, turquoise, a bead of patterned agate — rather than a chain.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kethreng*, literally "neck-string". Same ཕྲེང as ཕྲེང་བ, a mala — which the learner meets at District 8.

vocabulary.en_definition: The people next door or across the same courtyard. In a Tibetan town they are close to family in practice, in and out of the house without knocking.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khyimtshe*. "House-companion" — the ཁྱིམ is the same one in ཁྱིམ་ཚང `family`.

vocabulary.en_definition: Nepal — the country on the other side of the mountains, and the usual overland route in and out.
A Nepali person. Worth having early: much of the diaspora passed through Nepal, and in Lhasa the word is heard about traders.
Your brother's or sister's son. Aunts, uncles, nephews and nieces are close relations in a Tibetan family, often closer than the English words suggest.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshawo*. The same word as `grandchild` — not a homophone, the same word.

vocabulary.en_definition: New, said of goods rather than of news. It is what a stallholder says about their stock, and the word to listen for when you are being assured that something has not been sitting in a box since last year.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sarpa*. The ག is silent. Same word as in ལོ་གསར Losar, "new year".

vocabulary.en_definition: What has happened, whether from a broadcast or from whoever has just walked in. Over long distances the second kind still travels well.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sargyur*. New-change. གསར is the same syllable as ལོ་གསར, and the source points that out itself.

vocabulary.en_definition: Your brother's or sister's daughter, and the pair to nephew. The two are drilled together because they are used together.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshamo*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Night. The stretch after everything has closed, rather than a time you arrange to meet in.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshenmo*. The མ is a silent prefix. Same syllable as མཚན, `name` (H) — a real collision worth telling the learner about once.

vocabulary.en_definition: Nine. The last of the single digits, and the last piece you need before the tens.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gu*. The ད is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: Ninety. The last of the tens, and the top of the run before a hundred.
vocabulary.thl_note: *guchu*.

vocabulary.en_definition: The polite negative answer, for correcting a wrong guess about you without any sharpness. You will need it the first time someone assumes you are from somewhere you are not.
A herder of the high pastures, a drokpa. The word names a way of living, not the absence of a home.
vocabulary.thl_note: *drokpa*. Section 8.4 anchor — འབྲ is a single voiced *dr*, and the THL is fixed by `known-forms.json`, not derived.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Drokpa means roughly 'one of the high pastures', and it is half of a pair: the drokpa herds above the line where crops stop, the shingpa farms the valleys below. The two have traded for centuries, butter, cheese, wool and salt going down and barley coming up. A nomad family moves camp several times a year around a fixed round of pastures, which is not wandering; every move is to a place they already know.

vocabulary.en_definition: North. The four cardinal directions are taught here as one set, though on foot you will be given left, right and a landmark far more often than a compass point.
A monk who has taken the first set of vows but not the full ones. Novices are often young, and they are the ones most likely to be sent to walk a visitor round the buildings.
vocabulary.thl_note: *getshü*. The ད is a silent prefix and the ལ colours the vowel to ü rather than sounding.

vocabulary.en_definition: Now, at this moment. It is one of the most used words in any language and easy to skip past in a wordlist, and it turns up in nearly every arrangement you will hear made.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thaata*. ལྟ is a plain *ta*, and the whole word is heard as two light syllables — not "da l-ta".

vocabulary.en_definition: A woman who has taken monastic vows and lives in a nunnery community, in the same maroon robes as a monk. Nunneries are generally smaller than the men's monasteries and further from town.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Nunneries exist across Tibet and the Himalaya, some of them very old, and they have historically been smaller and poorer than the men's monasteries because they attracted less patronage. Full ordination for women was never established in the Tibetan tradition, so nuns hold novice vows; that has been argued over for decades, and some communities have taken the higher ordination elsewhere. In recent years the full debate curriculum and the geshema degree have been opened to nuns, which is new. A visitor is as welcome at a nunnery as at a monastery, and is usually shown round with more time to spare.

vocabulary.en_definition: Anything placed in front of an image — a lamp, a bowl of water, grain, a scarf, a folded note of money. The surface of a chapel altar is largely made of them.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhöpa*. Same silent མ and rounded vowel as མཆོད་མེ.

vocabulary.en_definition: The row of seven small bowls of water set out in front of a household shrine. They are filled in the morning and emptied in the evening, and the row is one of the first things you notice in a shrine room.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yönchhap*. ཆབ is the honorific word for water, which is why it is also inside ཆབ་གསང `toilet`.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The seven bowls offer a guest what a house would put in front of one: water to drink, water to wash with, flowers, incense, light, scented water and food. Plain water stands in for all of them because it is the one thing a household can give without limit, so nothing about the offering is grudging. They are filled with clean water each morning and set in a straight line with a small even gap — touching is avoided and so is spacing them widely. In the evening the water is poured out and the bowls are dried and stacked upside down, so the row is set up and taken down again every day of the year. Doing it is part of the ordinary running of a house rather than a specialist job, and it usually falls to whoever is up first.

vocabulary.en_definition: All right, fine, agreed. The general-purpose word for accepting what has been said or offered.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lakso* — the s of ལགས closes the syllable rather than starting a new one.

vocabulary.en_definition: Old, said of a person. It is not a rude word — age is respected, and stating it is ordinary.
One. The number you have already been using without knowing it, every time you ordered a single cup of anything.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chik*. Corroborated only inside sentences (`thengs gcig` once, `zhag po gcig` one day, `ki lo gcig` one kilo); the source has no number list.

vocabulary.en_definition: What somebody thinks about a question, as a thing you can ask for and give. It goes with 'What do you think?', which is the sentence that asks for one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *samtshü*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Outside. Its pair is inside, and it is often the honest answer about where a toilet is.
The bag carried on the back, holding everything for the journey. What goes in it is the first decision of any walk.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tophe*. The ལ prefix of ལྟོ is silent and the final ད of ཕད is not pronounced.

vocabulary.en_definition: Paper — a sheet of it, or the material in general.
A ceremonial parasol, one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The parasol stands for protection — shelter from suffering and from harm, the way a parasol shelters from sun. Real ones are carried over a lama in procession, so the symbol and the object are the same thing. Anywhere in Asia a parasol held over someone marked their standing, because it meant a person was employed to carry it, and in Buddhism that becomes protection. It is a parasol on a long handle, fringed and often silk.

vocabulary.en_definition: Anything sent that is not a letter. At the counter it gets weighed, and you may be asked to leave it open until it has been looked at.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thumdrak*. ཐུམ is "wrapped bundle" (ཐུམ་སྒྲིལ, to wrap up); the second syllable is the postal སྦྲག again.

vocabulary.en_definition: Both parents together, as a pair.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phama*. Father + mother, in that order — the opposite of the English pairing instinct.

vocabulary.en_definition: A park, and specifically the walled grove of trees a Lhasa family goes to for a whole day. It is less a municipal park than a picnic ground with a wall around it, and District 20 spends an afternoon in one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lingka* — གླ is a plain l, not "g-la".

vocabulary.en_definition: A high saddle between peaks, where a road crosses a range. On the plateau a pass, a la, is a named place with a marked summit rather than merely the top of a hill.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lakha*. ཁ here is "top, mouth of" — the top of the la, not a separate word to learn.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Crossing a pass is treated as a small arrival: the vehicle stops, everyone gets out into the wind, and the shout goes up. The summit carries a cairn of stones and a mass of prayer flags, and travelers add a stone as they cross. A pass is a named place with a marked summit rather than merely the top of a hill, and it is also where the weather turns and where the altitude is felt hardest.

vocabulary.en_definition: Peaches, which grow in the warmer valleys well below the plateau and mostly arrive up here dried. Fresh ones have a short season and are eaten close to where they grow.
A pencil.
vocabulary.thl_note: *shaanhyuk*. སྨྱུག is the same *nyuk* as in སྨྱུ་གུ — no "m", no "s".

vocabulary.en_definition: A person, in the general sense. Useful for counting people in a room or saying who a thing belongs to.
A pharmacy. There are two kinds in Lhasa, one selling manufactured medicine and one selling Tibetan medicine, and District 15 is about the second of them.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mhen tshongkhang* — སྨ is a plain m, the ས is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: A summer outing to a spot by water, with a tent, cooking gear and enough food for days. Nearer a small camp than a lunch.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lingka*. གླ is a single sound *l*, not "g" followed by "l" — the ག is a silent prefix. This is the *linka* of ནོར་བུ་གླིང་ག Norbulingka.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Around Lhasa the summer picnic is an institution rather than an outing: nearer a small camp than a lunch, and it can last a week. Visitors who wander past tend to be absorbed into whichever tent they are nearest, and declining the food takes considerably more effort than accepting it. Families put up a canvas tent in a park or a grove by the river and bring stoves, thermoses, cards and dice; the tents are white with blue appliqué patterns and go up in rows. The season runs through the warm months, when the barley is in the ground and there is a gap in the work.

vocabulary.en_definition: The pig, twelfth and last of the twelve, the animal the cycle ends on before starting again.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phakpa*. Aspirated *ph*, not an English *f*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Somebody who has travelled to a monastery or a holy place in order to be there. Many of the people in a monastery courtyard are pilgrims rather than local, and some have come a very long way.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nhekor wa*. Both the ག and the ས are silent prefixes — not "g-nas s-kor".

vocabulary.en_definition: The small brown-gray pills of Tibetan medicine, ground from plant and mineral ingredients and rolled by hand. They are the usual form a Tibetan prescription arrives in.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The herbal pill is the usual form a Tibetan prescription arrives in — small, brown-gray, and rolled by hand. The formulas are recorded in the medical texts and made up at the Men-Tsee-Khang, and larger pills are wrapped in coloured cloth and crushed or dissolved rather than swallowed whole. A pill is a compound rather than a single ingredient: many components, ground, blended to a written formula, rolled damp into a bead and dried. What any particular pill is for is a matter between a physician and a patient, and describing the form is as far as this goes.

vocabulary.en: the hall pillars, khatas tied to them
vocabulary.en_definition: One of the wooden pillars holding up the roof of the hall. They are worth naming because of what accumulates on them: visitors tie white scarves round the pillars, and the layers build up until the wood is hard to see.
The pillow on the bed. Asking for a second one is an ordinary request and is usually met.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nghego*. Both the ས of སྔས and the མ of མགོ are silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: Pink. The last of the everyday colors taught here, and the least likely to come up in a haggle.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mharkya*, literally "pale red" — the same formation as the source's སྔོ་སྐྱ "pale blue", with དམར་པོ's first syllable.

vocabulary.en_definition: A place, in the general sense. It is the word inside the question you use to ask where anything is.
A plate. Rather less used than the bowl, which does most of the work at a Tibetan table.
The word that softens a request. You always meet it inside a whole phrase in this track, so you never have to decide where to put it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *roknhang*. The dictionary's English→Tibetan hits for "please" (མགུ་བ, "to gratify") are the wrong sense entirely.

vocabulary.en_definition: A poem. Tibetan has a long written tradition of them and a parallel folk verse that is sung rather than read.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nhyenngak* / *nyen-ngak*. Two syllables, both with the ང sound; the ས prefix of སྙ is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: The counter where letters and parcels are sent. Also, in practice, where forms get filled in and where somebody will help you address something.
vocabulary.thl_note: *drakkhang*. The སྦྲ cluster is one low-tone onset — "dra", not "s-b-ra"; the same སྦྲག sits inside ཐུམ་སྦྲག (`parcel`) and སྦྲག་རྟགས (`stamp`), which is worth showing the learner as a family.

vocabulary.en_definition: The palace on the hill above the city, visible from most of it. It is the landmark visitors ask for most often and the easiest to steer by, because you can usually just look up and find it.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The Potala is the palace on the hill above Lhasa, visible from most of the city, and for many Tibetans it is the single image that stands for Tibet itself. From the seventeenth century it was the seat of the Tibetan government and the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas; it is a museum now. It climbs thirteen storeys on the site of a much older fort — the white outer sections held the offices and living quarters, the red block at the center the chapels and the tombs of eight Dalai Lamas. There is no steel in it and very little foundation: the walls are stone and rammed earth, metres thick at the base and tapering as they rise, which is what has kept it up.

vocabulary.en_definition: Potato. It grows well at altitude, so it is one of the vegetables that has always actually been here.

Prayer as a thing rather than an action — what is being said, and the general word for it. It covers what a hall of monks recites and what an old woman murmurs walking round the outside of the building.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mhönlam*. The ས is a silent prefix and the ན colours the vowel to ö.

vocabulary.en_definition: A pecha — a book of loose oblong leaves printed on both sides, stacked between two wooden boards and wrapped in cloth. It is not bound and does not open like a Western book.
vocabulary.thl_note: *pechha* — the English word for the object is borrowed from this one, so the card is teaching a word the learner may already own.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A pecha is not bound and does not open like a Western book: loose oblong leaves stacked between two wooden boards and wrapped in cloth. A reader unties the wrap, sets the stack down and moves each leaf aside as they finish it, so the book is worked through as a pile rather than turned. Pecha are kept high rather than on the floor, and are not stepped over or sat on. The format came from Indian palm-leaf manuscripts and kept the long narrow shape long after the material changed to paper, and the boards range from plain planks to carved and painted ones.

vocabulary.en_definition: A printed cloth flag, strung in long lines from rooftops, bridges and mountain passes, in a fixed sequence of five colors.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thaarchok*. ལྕ is a single *ch* — not "l" then "c".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Prayer flags are strung in long lines from rooftops, bridges and passes so that the wind moving over them carries the printing outward. They are meant to fade — cloth bleached blank by sun and wind has done its work, and new lines are strung over the old rather than the old taken down. The five colors run in a set order, blue, white, red, green and yellow, standing for sky, air, fire, water and earth, and each flag is block-printed with text and images. Passes are the densest place to see them, layered there by travelers over many years.

vocabulary.en_definition: A cylinder on a spindle with printed text rolled up inside it, turned by hand or set in rows along a wall to be turned by people passing.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mani khorlo*. The འ of འཁོར is silent — *khorlo*, not "'khor lo". ཎ is the retroflex n of the Sanskrit mantra and sounds like an ordinary n here.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A prayer wheel holds a tightly wound scroll printed with a mantra, and turning it is understood to have the same effect as saying what is inside. Rows of them run along monastery walls to be turned by anyone going past, which is what the stream of people beside them is doing. They are turned clockwise, the same direction as a kora, and sizes run from a hand wheel with a weighted chain to fixed wheels taller than a person, some of them driven by water.

vocabulary.en_definition: Before, previously, in the past. It points backwards without saying how far.
The price of a thing. In a market stall it is a starting position rather than a fact, which is what the second half of this district is about.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khoong*. Every haggling word in this district is built on it: གོང་ཆེན་པོ expensive, གོང་ཁེ་པོ cheap, གོང་ཆེ་དྲགས too expensive, གོང་བཅག cut the price.

vocabulary.en_definition: The full-length bow: down to the ground, arms stretched out in front, and up again. People do them on the spot along the kora, and some do them the whole way round, measuring the circuit with their own body.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhaktshe wa*. ཕྱ is a single sound *ch*, not "ph" + "y".
vocabulary.cultural_note: A prostration is a gesture of respect before anything else, made towards teachers and images rather than only at buildings. It goes hands together to the head, the throat and the heart, then down until the body is flat with the arms out, then up. Doing them in sets in one place is common, and the boards worn smooth outside a temple are where people do them; pilgrims prostrating along a road move forward by their own length each time, marking where their hands reached, which is how journeys of many months are made. Those covering ground wear wooden mitts and a leather apron rather than staying put. It is among the most photographed things in Tibet and among the easiest to photograph thoughtlessly, which is worth knowing before you raise a camera.

vocabulary.en_definition: Quality, as the thing being argued over. A haggle in the Barkhor runs on two axes, what it costs and how good it is, and this is the second one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *pü*. Almost never said bare — it appears bound, as སྤུས་དག་པོ "good quality".

vocabulary.en_definition: Quiet, said of a place: no traffic, no building work, no television through the wall. One of the two things most worth asking about a room.
A radio. In a camp a long way from anything else it is the thing left on in the background, and where the tent stands decides what it can pick up.
The big white winter radish, the size of a forearm, and the vegetable most reliably to hand in a kitchen here.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The white radish keeps through the winter without a cellar, which is what makes it the vegetable of a place with a long cold season and a short growing one. It goes into soup, into stews with meat, into momo filling, and it is cut into strips and dried on rooftops to keep it longer still. In a country where fresh vegetables were seasonal and often simply absent, it did the work that a whole vegetable aisle does elsewhere. It is still what you will see most of in a Lhasa market in February.

vocabulary.en_definition: Real, genuine. The single most useful adjective at a stone stall, and a polite one: the question is expected, and asking it is not treated as an accusation.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nghönhe*. Not an adjective in front of a noun — it sits before the copula: འདི་དངོས་གནས་རེད་པས། "is this real?", never དངོས་གནས་གཟི.

vocabulary.en_definition: The slip handed back afterwards, with a number on it that follows the parcel. Worth keeping until the thing has arrived at the other end.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dzinshok*. Hold-paper — the paper you keep. འཛིན་པ is "to hold, to grasp", which the source illustrates with བློ་ལ་འཛིན་པ, to keep in mind.

vocabulary.en_definition: Red. Part of the same set of five, and one of the most visible colors in any Tibetan town.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mharpo*. The ད is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Red is fire in the string of five prayer-flag colors, and it is the most visible color in any Tibetan town. It is the color of monastic robes and of the deep red bands painted across monastery walls, which is why a red building on a hillside is legible at a distance as what it is. Cloth dyed this red is sold everywhere in the Barkhor, and it is one of the colors you are most likely to actually want to ask for.

vocabulary.en_definition: A relative — anybody in the extended family, without specifying which. Useful precisely because the specific terms run deep and this one covers the rest.
vocabulary.thl_note: *pünkyak*. The ས is a silent prefix.

vocabulary.en_definition: A restaurant, usually a small room with a handful of tables and a short list of things it actually has.
vocabulary.thl_note: *saakhang*, "eating house" — the same ཁང as སྨན་ཁང (hospital) and འཛིན་ཁང (classroom).

vocabulary.en_definition: Rice. It is imported rather than grown at this altitude, so it is common in a town restaurant and rarer in a village.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dre*. The འ prefix is silent and the ས is not heard; an English reader will want "bras".

vocabulary.en_definition: Right. The other half of the pair, and worth being certain of before you set off following an answer.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yechhok*. Same silent ག as གཡོན.

vocabulary.en_definition: A road: something with traffic on it, big enough to be named. The larger of the two words you learn for a way through a town.
The maroon robes of a monk or a nun — several separate lengths of cloth wrapped and tucked rather than one garment put on. The color is what identifies the wearer from right across a courtyard.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thraachhe*. Same གྲ as in གྲྭ་པ: a single voiced *dr*, with the ྭ silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: The room you are given, and the word you use to ask for one. A guesthouse room is plain: beds, a window, a thermos of hot water on the floor.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khangmik*. The second syllable is the same མིག as in "eye" — the source glosses it that way; a room is a "house-hole".

vocabulary.en_definition: Rope, usually twisted from yak hair. A camp runs on it: guy lines, tethers and loads.

Said of a place, an object or a text that is treated as holy — approached in a particular way and not handled casually. A useful word for understanding why something is roped off, or why the room has gone quiet.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tsa chhenpo*. རྩ is a single *ts*, not "r" then "tsa".

vocabulary.en_definition: A riding saddle built up at front and back on a wooden frame, and covered with rugs.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ga*, one syllable. Homograph warning: སྒ is also the word for ginger, which is what every dictionary in the cache returns for it.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A saddle is the piece of a herder's equipment most likely to be decorated, and a good one is handed down rather than replaced. It is dressed for a festival the way a rider is: worked metal at the front and back, and saddle rugs in bands of color under and over it. The frame is wooden, built high at front and back so that a rider sits into it rather than on top of it, which is what makes a long day in it possible. Motorbikes have taken over much of the daily herding, so a full set of saddle and rugs now comes out mostly for racing and for festivals.

vocabulary.en_definition: Salt. In tea it is deliberate rather than a mistake, and knowing that in advance saves a learner one bad surprise.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tsha*. One syllable. The subscript ྭ is not pronounced as a w — and the source itself warns about the collision: ཚྭ *tsa* salt against ཚ *tsha* hot, which the learner meets on the very next card as ཚ་པོ.

vocabulary.en_definition: Salty. Butter tea is, deliberately, and that is usually the first thing a newcomer notices about it. Keep it apart from salt itself, which is the substance rather than the quality.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshakhu*. ཚྭ is the `salt` card; ཁུ the source glosses as broth or fluid — "salt-broth", so the word describes the liquid rather than the taste.

vocabulary.en_definition: A sacred design made from coloured sand, built and then deliberately swept away.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A sand mandala is swept up when it is finished and the sand carried to a river — that is the teaching, not an afterthought. Something made this beautifully and this slowly is still let go, because everything is. It is a sacred design made from thousands of grains of coloured sand, laid down through a narrow metal funnel. Monks may work on one for days or weeks, and every line follows a set plan rather than an artist's choice.

vocabulary.en_definition: Saturday, the day of Saturn, as in English. It carries the card for the whole set of seven.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The seven day names are also people's names: Nyima, Dawa, Lhakpa, Phurbu, Pasang and Penpa are all common, traditionally given for the day a person was born. So learning the seven gives you a week of days and a week of names at the same time. The Tibetan week runs Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn — the same seven bodies in the same order as the European week, which is why Tuesday to Friday line up with the French names exactly.

vocabulary.en_definition: The written form of the language — the shapes themselves, as distinct from the words they spell. Tibetan has one alphabet, written in more than one hand.
vocabulary.thl_note: *yiksuuk*. གཟུགས is *suk* — the ག prefix is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tibetan script carries a standing well beyond reading: letters are carved into rock, painted on cliffs and printed on cloth where nobody expects to read closely. There is one alphabet written in two broad styles — an upright printed form and a faster cursive one — and the same thirty letters serve both. It was devised in the seventh century on an Indian model and has changed very little since, which is a large part of why spelling and speech have drifted so far apart. It is also used for several other languages of the region, and it is more regular than it looks, because the same shapes repeat.

vocabulary.en_definition: Seven. It counts the days of the week, which you meet properly much later on.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dün*. The final ན is nasalisation, not a consonant.

vocabulary.en_definition: Seventy. One of the tens you are more likely to hear than to say.
vocabulary.thl_note: *dünchu*.

vocabulary.en_definition: A flat round pastry stuffed with minced meat and fried. It is the thing eaten with tea, and in many teahouses it is the only food on the counter.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sha phaaklep*. Literally meat-bread: ཤ meat + བག་ལེབ bread, both of which the source teaches separately.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Shabaley is what is eaten with tea, and in many teahouses it is the only food on the counter. It is one of very few Tibetan dishes that is street food rather than something a family makes at home, cooked in front of you in a wide pan of oil and eaten standing up. A disc of dough is sealed around spiced minced beef, crimped shut at the edge and shallow-fried until the surface blisters, so it comes out somewhere between a pie and a fritter. The name travels with the food and gets written several different ways on menus in Lhasa, in Dharamsala and in Queens, none of which is wrong.

vocabulary.en_definition: Sheep, kept in flocks alongside the yak herd for wool, milk and meat.
A shirt. Worn under a chuba as often as on its own.
vocabulary.thl_note: *töthung*, literally "upper-short".

vocabulary.en_definition: Sho, the dice game played across teahouse tables. It is the second thing happening in the room after conversation, and the noise of it is the sound of the place from the street.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sho*. One syllable, and the game is ཤོ་རྒྱག་པ *sho gyakpa* — the same རྒྱག verbaliser the source uses for playing cards.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Sho is the dice game played across teahouse tables, and after conversation it is the second thing happening in the room. Players call out as they throw, in set phrases and often in rhyme, and the calling is half the game — a good player is entertaining as well as fortunate. The dice are thrown from a wooden cup slammed down onto a leather pad, with shells or coins moved around the rim as counters, and the slam is what makes a teahouse audible from the street. It is largely a men's game and largely an afternoon one, small amounts of money change hands, and somebody standing and watching is welcome as long as they are not in the way of the throw.

vocabulary.en_definition: Shoes. General footwear, of the kind stacked on any market table.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lhamkok*.

vocabulary.en_definition: A shop or a stall. The Barkhor is mostly the second kind: a table, an awning and a great deal of stock.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshongkhang*, literally "selling-house". ཁང is the same element as in D3's buildings.

vocabulary.en_definition: The shopkeeper or stallholder. The person you are about to spend ten friendly minutes disagreeing with about a price.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshongpön*, literally "selling-chief". Not honorific in itself — you make it polite by adding ལགས when you address them.

vocabulary.en_definition: The room in a house kept for the family shrine. It is usually the best room in the building, and it is not a spare room used for other things.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhökhang*. མཆོད is *chö* — the མ is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Most Tibetan households keep a room, or at minimum a wall, for the shrine, and it is very rarely absent altogether. It generally gets the best light and the best carpets in the house, and formal guests are received there. The altar holds images, photographs of teachers, butter lamps, and seven small bowls of water set out in the morning and emptied at night. The daily upkeep falls to whoever is at home rather than to a specialist, and in a small flat the whole thing shrinks to a shelf.

vocabulary.en_definition: Your name written in your own hand, which is what the counter wants before a parcel goes. Older documents were closed with a stamped seal instead, and seals have not entirely disappeared.
vocabulary.thl_note: *mingtak*. Name-mark. རྟགས is the same "sign" syllable as in ལག་རྟགས (gift) and སྦྲག་རྟགས (`stamp`), which gives this district three words built on it.

vocabulary.en_definition: Silk. At the cloth stalls it usually means the heavy patterned brocade used to trim a chuba, edge a hat or mount a painting, rather than a plain bolt of the stuff.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thaarkö*. དར is the same element as in དར་ལྕོག, prayer flags — the learner meets it again at District 8.

vocabulary.en_definition: Silver. Nearly all Tibetan jewelry is set in it, and the stalls selling stones sell them already mounted rather than loose. The word comes back in District 19, where you meet the people who work it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nghü* — the same word as `money`, not a homophone. Tibetan money is named after the metal.

vocabulary.en_definition: Someone who sings, whether or not it is their living. Being asked to sing at a gathering is ordinary here, and most people have something ready.
Six. Halfway through the run that everything larger is built out of.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thruuk*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Sixty. Prices climb through here fast, so the tens are worth more drilling than the digits.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thruukchu*. ཅུ here, not བཅུ — sixty, seventy and eighty take ཅུ, forty, fifty and ninety take བཅུ. That is orthography, not a difference you can hear.

vocabulary.en_definition: Size. It sits inside asking for a bigger one, and clothes at a stall are sorted by rough size rather than by any number, so the word does more work here than a measurement would.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhechhung*, literally "big-small". It is this district's own `big` and `small` fused into one noun, which is worth showing the learner rather than hiding.

vocabulary.en_definition: The sky. In the five-color sequence on a prayer flag it is the blue one, and it comes first in the order.
vocabulary.thl_note: *namkha*. The final འ is silent; མཁ is an aspirated *kh*.

vocabulary.en_definition: A woven wool sling, used to throw a stone past the herd so that the animals turn without being touched.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The sling is how a herder steers: a stone landed beyond an animal, on the side it should move away from, turns the herd without anything being touched. Often the crack of it in the air is enough on its own. Slings are woven from wool in patterned bands and worn round the waist or over the shoulder, so they serve as a belt when they are not in use.

vocabulary.en_definition: Slowly. It is a word in its own right, and it also sits inside both goodbyes, which is why learning it stops them being two opaque noises.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khaaler*. The ག is unvoiced at the start of a word.

vocabulary.en_definition: Small. The other half of the pair, and the more common complaint of the two: clothes bought off a stall run smaller than most visitors expect.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhungchhung*. Reduplicated, unlike ཆེན་པོ — the pair is not symmetrical in Tibetan the way big/small is in English.

vocabulary.en_definition: Something light eaten between meals rather than a meal itself. The street food in this district — the fried pastry, the cold noodle — belongs here rather than under lunch.
The snow leopard: the pale gray, heavy-tailed cat of the high crags. Herders know it as the animal that takes livestock, and almost nobody, herders included, ever sees one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sa*, one syllable — the ' is the འ suffix and is not a glottal stop for the learner to produce.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Herders know the snow leopard as the animal that takes livestock, and almost nobody, herders included, ever sees one. It lives mostly on blue sheep, hunting by getting above them on a slope and dropping, and takes goats when wild prey is thin, which is where the trouble with herders begins. The tail is nearly as long as the animal, used for balance on rock and wrapped around itself when it lies down, and it cannot roar — the noises it makes are closer to a house cat's than to a lion's. Some monasteries have long forbidden hunting on the mountains behind them, and surveys have found a meaningful share of the plateau's cats living on exactly that ground.

vocabulary.en_definition: The snow lion: white, with a turquoise mane, and an emblem rather than an animal anybody has met. It is on flags and carvings and holding up the thrones inside temples.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khaang sengke*. The ས of གངས is silent.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The snow lion is an emblem rather than an animal anybody has met: white, with a turquoise mane, holding up the thrones inside temples and standing on flags and carvings. It appears in pairs far more often than singly — two hold up a throne, two flank a doorway, two face each other on old Tibetan coins. The mane and the eyebrows are turquoise, which is the quickest way to tell it from any other carved beast on a beam. It is one of the four figures at the corners of a windhorse print, alongside the tiger, the garuda and the dragon, and there is a dance for it as well, performed by two people inside a single costume.

vocabulary.en_definition: A permanently snow-capped peak. It is its own category in Tibetan rather than a mountain that happens to have snow on it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khaangri*. The ས of གངས is silent and nasalises into the ར.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A snow mountain is treated as the residence of a local deity and the protector of the district below, so a peak is a neighbor addressed by name rather than scenery. Villages orient themselves by their peak, and it is often the first thing named when someone tells you where they are from. It is its own category in Tibetan rather than a mountain that happens to have snow on it, and several are, by local preference, not climbed at all.

vocabulary.en_definition: Soap for washing. Like the towel, more often something you bring than something you find waiting.
Socks. Not glamorous, and sold on every second table in the market.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kangshup*, literally "foot-casing" — the same ཤུབས as ལག་ཤུབས gloves.

vocabulary.en_definition: A son — yours or somebody else's.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phuu*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Sorry. An apology for something you did or bumped into, rather than a way of getting attention.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gongtak*. The དག prefix is silent; not "d-gongs d-ag".

vocabulary.en_definition: Soup or broth. It is the base of the district's best-known dish and a course in its own right.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thang*, one syllable. Not the ཐང of ཐང་ཆད ("tired").

vocabulary.en_definition: South. It appears inside place names rather more than inside directions, which is a good enough reason on its own to recognize it.
Something kept for where it came from rather than what it does — a photograph, a length of cloth, a stone picked up on a pass.
vocabulary.thl_note: *threenten*. Same དྲན as District 9's `memory` དྲན་པ — a keepsake is literally a support for remembering.

vocabulary.en_definition: Spelling: which letters go into a word, as against how the word sounds. In Tibetan those two things sit much further apart than in English, which is why spelling is the genuinely hard part of school here.
vocabulary.thl_note: *djorlok*. སྦྱ is a single *j* — no "s", no "b". ཀློ is *lo*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Spicy, hot with chilli. Worth having before you order rather than after, which is why it is taught with the phrase for asking against it.
vocabulary.thl_note: Literally "hot-mouthed", not "hot" — ཚ་པོ alone is the temperature word, and the ཁ is what makes it about chilli.

vocabulary.en_definition: A spoon. What arrives with soup, and often the only utensil on the table.
The steps between one level and the next. Guesthouse stairs are commonly steep, narrow, and outside in the courtyard rather than indoors.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kedzek*. The ས of སྐས is a silent prefix, and འཛ is a single *dz*.

vocabulary.en_definition: The bus station: a yard of parked buses and vans, a ticket window, and people waiting with their bags.
vocabulary.thl_note: *baptshuk*. The འ is a silent prefix.

vocabulary.en_definition: A cast or molded image standing on the altar of a chapel. Most are gilded, dressed in real cloth, and considerably older than they look.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kudra* — heard as *ku-dra*. The ས prefix is silent and འདྲ is a single voiced *dra*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Steam, off a pot or a kettle or a stack of momo trays. Useful because it is the sign that something is ready, and the reason behind 'Careful, it's hot'.
The stove in the main room — cooking, heating and the place everybody sits around, all at once. It is where the family is, so it is where a guest is taken.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thap*. Also the ཐབ inside ཐབ་ཚང, kitchen.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The stove is where the family is, so it is where a guest is taken: cooking, heating and the place everybody sits around, all at once. Its position sets the seating order — the places nearest the warmth go to elders and to guests, and being moved towards it is being honoured. The traditional stove burns dung or wood and stands at or near the center of the main room, which is the one reliably warm spot in a house with no other heating, and tea is kept hot on it all day. Bottled gas and electric rings have arrived in the towns, but the arrangement of a room around its center has not changed much.

vocabulary.en_definition: Straight ahead. The most common answer to where is it, usually accompanied by a flat hand pointing down the street.
vocabulary.thl_note: *shar gyak* — རྒྱག is *gyak*, not "r-gyag".

vocabulary.en_definition: A street, of the kind the old town is made of. Narrower than a road and usually busier on foot.

Strong, said of a person: physically strong, and by extension able to keep going. It is used approvingly about people who work outdoors, which on the plateau is most people, and it is warmer than it sounds in English.
Sunday. The Tibetan name for the day is built on the Sun, exactly as the English one is.
Black tea boiled with milk and sugar, served by the glass. It is the other tea, and in a Lhasa teahouse it is what most people are drinking.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Sweet tea is what most people in a Lhasa teahouse are actually drinking: black tea boiled with milk and sugar, served by the glass. The teahouses run on a simple arrangement — you sit, put coins on the table, and someone comes past with a thermos, filling your glass and taking payment from the pile. It came over the Himalaya from India and Nepal rather than out of the older Tibetan kitchen, and has been so thoroughly adopted that an afternoon can be spent on very little, which is what these places are for.

vocabulary.en_definition: Sweets, biscuits and the like, kept in a bowl and pressed on anybody who comes in. Refusing once is expected and will not stop the offering.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhiiri*. བྱི is *ji*, not "b" followed by "y".

vocabulary.en_definition: Switzerland. It is on this short list for a reason: the largest Tibetan community in Europe is there, and a Tibetan you meet may well have relatives in it.
A table. In a teahouse it is low, long and shared, and it belongs to the room rather than to you. The same word does duty in the restaurant and the guesthouse later on.
vocabulary.thl_note: *choktse*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Someone who makes clothes to measure. A chuba is cut for the person who will wear it, so this is an everyday trade rather than a luxury one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshem phuu khen*. The final ན of མཁན is nasal, not a hard n.

vocabulary.en_definition: The all-purpose greeting, safe with anyone at any hour of the day. It is the first thing you will say off the bus and the last thing you will stop needing.
vocabulary.cultural_note: It is a good wish rather than a report on the time of day, which is why one form covers morning, evening and every stranger in between. The same words carry the New Year, so it always keeps a faint edge of celebration. Said with a small bow of the head it becomes formal; said quickly across a market stall it is ordinary courtesy.

vocabulary.en_definition: Taste or flavor, as a noun. It is what you comment on when someone asks how the food is, and it comes back with the rest of the taste words in the kitchen district.
Tea in general. Said on its own in a teahouse it will usually get you butter tea, so it is rarely as neutral a word as it looks.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhaa*. One letter, one syllable — and it is the first syllable of almost every other card in this district: ཇ་མངར་མོ, ཇ་ཐང, ཇ་དམ, ཇ་ཁང.

vocabulary.en_definition: The bowl a person drinks tea from, often wooden and personal to them.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The tea bowl is personal: people carried their own inside the fold of the chuba and used it wherever they went. Your host refilling it before it is empty is not impatience, it is the ordinary courtesy of the room. It is a shallow wooden bowl, and the thing Tibetan butter tea is actually drunk from. A good one is turned from a burl and can be extremely valuable; a plain one is an everyday object.

vocabulary.en_definition: The teahouse itself: a room with benches, thermoses and a great deal of conversation. It is a social place more than a catering one.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhaakhang*. ཁང is the same syllable as in every other building word — the source lists ཟ་ཁང restaurant, དངུལ་ཁང bank, སྨན་ཁང hospital, འཛིན་ཁང classroom.

vocabulary.en_definition: A telephone as a fixed device — the one on a desk or in a shop, as opposed to the one in your pocket.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khapar*. The spoken source glosses it literally — "mouth picture" — and the learner meets the same word again whole inside ཁ་པར་ཨང་གྲངས (`phone-number`), which is the reason for the change below.

vocabulary.en_definition: A building where images are kept and where people come to make offerings. Inside a monastery it is one building among several rather than the whole place.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lhakhang*. ལྷ is one sound, an aspirated *lh*, not "l" then "h".

vocabulary.en_definition: Ten. The joint the whole counting system turns on: the numbers above it are built openly out of ten and the digits you have just learned.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chu*. The བ is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: Noodle soup made with dough torn into rough squares by hand rather than cut into strands. It is heavier and more homely than thukpa, and it is what gets cooked when the weather turns.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thenthuk*, from འཐེན་པ "to pull" — the noodles are pulled by hand, which is the whole difference from thukpa.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tenthuk is what gets cooked when the weather turns: noodle soup made with dough torn into rough squares by hand rather than cut into strands. It belongs to the household more than to the restaurant, which is why a bowl of it in somebody's kitchen is reliably better than a bowl of it on a menu. The dough is rolled flat then pulled and pinched straight into the boiling broth, so no two pieces are the same shape and the soup thickens as it goes. It sits inside the thukpa family rather than beside it: the name is what distinguishes the torn kind from the rest.

vocabulary.en_definition: A painting on cloth, mounted in a brocade surround with a dowel at the bottom so that it can be rolled up and carried. They hang in temples and in the shrine room of a house.
vocabulary.cultural_note: A thangka is a painting on cloth that rolls — mounted in brocade with a dowel at the bottom, so it travels, which mattered in a country of long journeys. They hang in temples and in the shrine room of a house, behind a silk curtain that is lifted to show the painting rather than left open. It is painted on primed cotton to a measured grid: the proportions of each figure are set by manuals, so the painter's freedom lies in the landscape, the color and the fineness of the line rather than in the composition. Mineral pigments, and powdered gold on the expensive ones, give them their depth.

vocabulary.en_definition: A painter of thangkas — the cloth scroll paintings that hang in temples and homes. The work is drawing and colouring to a set plan rather than composing a picture.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lha dri pa*. འབྲི is a voiced *dri*, not "b" followed by "r".
vocabulary.cultural_note: A painter trains for years under one master, starting with grinding pigment and ruling grids before touching a figure. The proportions of each figure are fixed by an iconometric system, measured outward in units from the face, so the painter's judgement goes into line, color and detail rather than layout — being correct matters more than being original. Pigments are mineral, ground and mixed in the workshop, and gold is applied last and burnished. A finished painting is not framed but mounted in brocade, with a cloth cover that folds down over the front.

vocabulary.en_definition: Thank you. The words are literally "great kindness", which is why it can sound warmer than the English and is worth using more often, not less.
That one, the thing over there or behind the stallholder. The pair to this, and just as much used.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thee*. Same position as འདི, after the noun. The plural is དེ་ཚོ, which the source uses constantly (`rkang shubs 'di tsho`).

vocabulary.en_definition: There, away from you. The other half of the pointing, and the word inside it's over there.
The thermos flask that stands on the table and does the refilling. It is the single most present object in this district.
vocabulary.cultural_note: The thermos is the most present object in a Tibetan room: it holds the tea, so tea is available continuously and without ceremony. Almost every table, kitchen, shop counter and long-distance bus has one, and a guest arriving is a thermos being lifted. They are usually enamelled or painted with flowers and kept full from morning to night, and refilling a cup costs nobody anything, which is why it happens constantly.

vocabulary.en_definition: These days, lately. It frames what is true now against what used to be, and it opens a great many conversations about home.
Thin, said of a person. The pair to fat, and equally sayable out loud.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sha kampo*. Literally "dry-fleshed". སྐ is *k*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Thirsty. The air on the plateau is dry enough that you will be for most of the day, which is part of why tea is put in front of you constantly. Its partner, hungry, arrives in the next district.
Thirty. Like the rest of the tens, it is built from a digit you already know and the word for ten.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sumchu*. གསུམ loses its ག prefix in the compound — སུམ, not གསུམ.

vocabulary.en_definition: This one, the thing near you or in your hand. Half of a market transaction is done by pointing and this is the word that goes with the finger.
vocabulary.thl_note: *di*. It follows its noun — ཞྭ་མོ་འདི "this hat", never འདི་ཞྭ་མོ.

vocabulary.en_definition: A thought — a single one, the kind that arrives and passes. Grouped here with dream and memory as things that happen in the heart-mind.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sampo*. The བ of བསམ is a silent prefix and བློ is *lo*.

vocabulary.en_definition: One thousand. For the larger things: a coat, a rug, a night somewhere.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhiktong*. གཅིག appears here as ཆིག — the same reduction as in ཆིག་བརྒྱ.

vocabulary.en_definition: Three. From here on the numbers are mostly a matter of hearing them said quickly enough to catch.
vocabulary.thl_note: *sum*. The ག is silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: The raised seat at the front of a hall, kept for the teacher who sits there. It stays in place and stays empty when he is not present, which visitors sometimes read as neglect when it is the opposite.
vocabulary.thl_note: *shuukthri*. བཞ is a single *sh* with the བ silent, and ཁྲི is *tri*, not "kh" then "r".

vocabulary.en_definition: Noodle soup: broth, noodles, some meat or vegetables, served scalding in a deep bowl. The ordinary evening meal.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Thukpa is the ordinary evening meal: noodles in broth with some meat or vegetables, served scalding in a deep bowl. It is winter food in a place with a long winter, and a bowl of it is the standard answer to somebody arriving cold and late. It is a family of dishes rather than one recipe — noodles pulled long, cut short, or torn into rough squares — and every household makes it slightly differently and is confident theirs is correct.

vocabulary.en_definition: Thursday, the day of Jupiter, the planet behind the French jeudi.
Tibet: the plateau this whole walk is set on, most of it lying above four thousand metres.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phöö*. The ད is silent and colours the vowel; not "bod".
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tibet is the highest inhabited region on earth, a plateau ringed by the Himalaya on one side and desert on the others, where altitude decides what grows and what is eaten. So the staple is barley rather than rice, the fat butter rather than oil, and tea is drunk salted and hot all day. It is also large enough that the Tibetan of one valley is hard work for someone from another, and for many Tibetans abroad it is a place they are from and have never been.

vocabulary.en_definition: The Tibetan language: the thing you are learning, and the name to give it when somebody asks what you are studying.
vocabulary.cultural_note: Tibetan is not related to Chinese. It belongs to the Tibeto-Burman family, and it is written in its own script, adapted in the seventh century from an Indian model. Spoken Tibetan varies enormously across the plateau — a herder from Amdo and a shopkeeper in Lhasa can struggle to follow each other — and what this app teaches is the Lhasa speech that works as the common tongue. The written language has stayed close enough to its classical form that a thousand-year-old text is still legible to a reader today, which is one reason the script and the speech are taught here as two separate walks.

vocabulary.en_definition: A Tibetan person. You will hear it as a question about yourself more often than you expect, especially if you look as though you might be.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phööpa*. The ད is silent and colours the vowel to ö.
